entries.text: Day One (Cumulative) — Twenty-four attended hours across your career. The deck calls this dedication.
Billable Hour — One full attended hour. HR has logged your enthusiasm.
Serial Founder — Five exits. At this point the exits are the product.
Out of the Garage — Crossed your first tier gate. The commemorative plaque is already being engraved.
Burn Rate — Spent 1e9 cash crossing a single gate. The board calls this investing in growth.
Server Farm — One hundred beige towers. The hum is audible from the parking lot.
Beige at Scale — Three hundred beige towers. Nobody remembers what the first one does.
CAPEX — Bought your first generator. It began depreciating before the receipt printed.
Procurement Pipeline — Twenty-five generators purchased. The vendor sent a gift basket.
Enterprise Refresh — Twenty-five generators in one Tier-3 run. The old ones were fine.
Exit Interview — Completed your first exit. You kept the hoodie.
Verified by possession: the game checked what you own right now. It did not ask how, and it will not ask again.
Hyperscale — Reached Tier 5. Your infrastructure has infrastructure.
First attempt. The comparison column stays empty until there is a personal best to compare.
This counter is real. It counts everyone here right now, one at a time. Each one is a person.
Decorative armor for a horse. You do not have a horse. Price: {price}, forever.
In 2006, armor like this cost real money and changed the industry. Ours is free, does nothing, and always will. That is the whole joke.

Someone with a bigger office read your rate sheet and made an offer for the people, not the product. The product was turned off on a Tuesday. You are told this is a success, and by every metric that gets published, it is.
You bought the future faster than the present could pay for it. The machines are still warm. Statistically, this is the most realistic thing in this game.
Nothing here ran unless you were touching it, so what you actually built was a job. The pivot is the part where you admit that and keep the contacts.
Your first company failed. Statistically, this is the most realistic thing in this game. Everything it taught you survives it — see below.
The second company gets founded by someone who has already failed once. Historically, that is the good kind of founder.
You have two hands. The meter refills on its own, free, always. It is a speed limit, not a store.
The offer lapsed, unanswered. The company is still yours.
Offer accepted. The rest is paperwork.
An offer is on the table: {exit_type}. It stands until {expires_at_ms}.
Takes jobs while you're out!! Every blink of the red light is a neighbor who didn't hang up.
The computer. Beige, sturdy, warm on top. It fixes the small jobs by itself while you handle the big ones.
Provisioned towers stop at the printed limit. Every cap in this program is a number you can read.
Procurement now orders towers by itself, on a schedule. You signed something. New Beige Towers just arrive.
Six monitors on one desk. Nothing requires six monitors. Investors require you to have six monitors.
Invoices print all night on tractor-feed paper. The rip along the perforation is the sound of getting paid!!
Employee #2, paid partly in options. The handshake felt historic to both of you. Everything goes further with two of you.
A real server rack in the garage, between the paint cans and the bikes. The plaque out front calls it a data center.
Files permits, slowly, correctly. Also accumulates institutional knowledge, most of which is the word no.
Your sister's kid. Great with computers. Paid in pizza and experience. Keeps a stack of finished jobs ready for Monday.
One repair, one dollar, one happy neighbor. This is the whole business right now. It is honest work.
Cash is capped. The cap is a number, the number is visible, and nothing will ever sell you the difference.
The county issues at most 24 concurrent permits. The county does not care about your roadmap.
Thank you, {founder}!! Your {price} has been processed. Nothing will ship. You already had everything.
There is nothing to buy. There will never be anything to buy. This form is the whole store.

==========================================================================
  CLOUD CLICKER 1.0                                            README.TXT
==========================================================================

  Thank you for downloading this program!! It means a lot. Really.

  WHAT THIS IS
  ------------
  A small business simulator. You fix computers for your neighbors,
  one dollar at a time, and you see where that goes. (It goes
  somewhere. The title bar knows more than it is saying.)

  HOW TO PLAY
  -----------
  Click FIX COMPUTER. Buy equipment when you can afford it. Your
  equipment keeps working while you are away -- at ninety percent,
  for up to a day, the way the door games on the BBS shared one phone line.
  They called that fairness. So do we.

  REGISTRATION
  ------------
  This program is free. Not free-to-play. Not free-with-purchases.
  Free. There is no registered version, because there is nothing to
  register against. If you would like the full experience of paying,
  print ORDER.FRM and mail us zero dollars. Postage neither included nor
  required.

  WISHLIST (things we are saving up for)
  --------------------------------------
  * an office with a door
  * a second phone line
  * whatever comes after all this  (see: OUR VISION, slide 1 of 1)

  KNOWN ISSUES
  ------------
  * The timer in the title bar counts something that has not been
    explained to you yet. This is intentional. It will be.
  * The visitor counter is real. We cannot fix that. We would not.

  GREETZ
  ------
  To every sysop, every beta tester, everyone who mailed a bug
  report on paper, and whoever invented the perforated edge.

                                            -- the authors, nineteen ninety-five
==========================================================================
The trial never ends and registers nothing. In 1995 this screen asked for $25 and a stamp. We ask for neither. We just liked the screen.
The deadline is real; the terms will not improve or worsen while you decide. This timer is information, not pressure.
Someone wants to buy the company. The full terms are below — all of them. Nothing on this sheet is hidden.
Attended time: {attended}. The clock only counted while you were actually here.
The company is over. The Founder is not. Everything below carries forward.
OFFLINE — the server did not pick up. You can play on this machine only for now.
One dashboard. One number. A world that runs itself — optimized, forever.
Free forever. No purchases. No ads. The only thing this game harvests is the fictional planet.
This account is anonymous and complete. An email, if you ever add one, is only a spare key.
OFFLINE — progress is parked on this machine until the server picks up again.
Watch the disk come gently back into order.
You gave yourself time to recover.
Repot the server-room plants. There is no streak to keep.
You stopped long enough to care for something.
Sit among the quiet racks. Arrange things if you feel like it.
Nothing needed you for a while.
The server needs a minute. Your equipment keeps working while it's away, and nothing is lost. Back soon!!

era_variants.era_2000: Scheduled maintenance in progress. Production continues server-side. Uptime is our passion.

entries.text: While you were away the machine kept working at {rate_percent}%, up to {cap_hours} hours. BBS door games did this first, because everyone shared one phone line. They called it fairness. So do we.
The two copies of the books disagreed, so everything was recounted. The server's copy wins. It always does. Nothing was lost.
Clout carries. The personal brand survives the company.
Spare RAM in a shoebox under the desk. The tower finds everything twice as fast now.
Five thousand sheets, all attached to each other. The printer never stops to reload. Neither, it turns out, do the invoices.
THUNK. The screen wobbles, settles, perfect. Officially it is maintenance. Unofficially everyone takes a turn.
Forty pages. Page one says 'we're like a family here.' The other thirty-nine are about liability.
Licensed fair and square from a man with a keyboard. Callers wait twice as long, contentedly. It's a waltz.
Where everything is, finally written down — in one binder, by the one person who knew. She is no longer load-bearing.
Five hundred cards, raised lettering. He hands them to everyone he meets. It works. Nobody can explain why it works.
Every server now slides into every rack. One meeting decided this. It was the company's best meeting, and its last short one.
The same machine, plus a sticker. It sells for twice as much now. Write this trick down; the industry will.
One keystroke answers every message at once, mostly with 'Received!!'. Twice the correspondence, twice the business.
